claims.text: Machine-learning potentials trained on ab initio data can determine melting temperatures across the high-entropy-alloy family accurately and efficiently.
Such potentials can accurately and efficiently determine enthalpies and entropies of fusion across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Such potentials can accurately and efficiently determine volume changes at melting across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Such potentials can accurately and efficiently determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
DFT or AIMD calculations can supply the ab initio training data for the machine-learning potentials.
High-entropy alloys typically melt between 1000 K and 2000 K.
The machine-learning potentials influence or represent atomic arrangements and bonding in the high-entropy alloy.
Capturing complex interatomic interactions and correlations enables accurate prediction of high-entropy-alloy thermodynamic properties.
The average absolute prediction error for the listed melting and liquid-state properties will be below 5% relative to experiments or first-principles calculations.
The proposed approach applies to high-entropy alloys containing three to six principal elements.
The proposed approach applies when constituent concentrations are between 5 at.% and 35 at.%.
Model transferability to previously unseen high-entropy alloys may be limited.
Experimental reference values used for validation may themselves be uncertain.
The approach is falsified if prediction error exceeds 10% for more than 20% of the tested alloys.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims performance 'across the high-entropy-alloy family,' whereas the boundary restricts applicability to alloys with three to six principal elements and constituent concentrations of 5–35 at.%; the unrestricted family-wide wording is therefore inconsistent with the stated scope.
